One of the recurring themes of Duke Ellington's career was pushing against boundaries once he came up against them.

Not racial boundaries, particularly. He was happy to work with black or white musicians, so long as they were good, but he wasn't a bomb-throwing rabble-rousing social change advocate. He carried himself with class, and did a soft-shoe routine around the prejudices of others. For example, when his orchestra toured the Jim Crow South in the '30s and '40s, instead of trying to deal with the headaches of hotels suddenly "losing" reservations, or having angry hooded mobs barring entry to said hotels, he rented Pullman cars, and had his boys sleep in the cars at the train stations. Clever, non-confrontational, and still getting his music to those who wanted to hear it; this was how he handled potential controversies through most of his life.

But technical and musical boundaries chafed him, and he kept finding ways to bypass those, sometimes successfully, sometimes less so.

This piece was both a protest against the hard three-minute (and twenty or thirty seconds) limit of 78 rpm records, which limited pop and jazz compositions to that length, and a bid for greater respectability (a craving he carried the rest of his life as well).

"Reminiscing In Tempo" is the first long-form piece Ellington composed. The idea behind it is a man sitting quietly, looking back on his life, good times and bad, and all the moods that that would imply, but every mood, every memory, keeps to exactly the same tempo. (It was also colored by the death of his beloved mother earlier in the year.)

The finished piece covered four sides of 10-inch 78 records, an extravagance his record company only put up with because his band was so popular.

Some afficionados say it is also his best long-form piece, because it is consistent from beginning to end.

This experimentation and exploration beyond boundaries took place even as swing, which was only christened as "swing" around 1934, was about to become the popular form of music in the nation. Ellington's orchestra, and his compositions, can be said to be the most direct fathers to swing, but it was the white Benny Goodman who turned it into a national craze.

Some historians, notably Ken Burns, have made insinuations about how Ellington "must have felt", seeing a white boy crowned "the King of Swing", but Ellington rarely badmouthed musicians of any stripe, and if he was jealous, it seems to have been on a much more limited scale, such as wishing that he had played Carnegie Hall before Goodman, which didn't happen. (Ellington played Carnegie far more often than Goodman, who only did so twice; one imagines that was at least some kind of consolation.)

I'll certainly return to Ellington, but if one wants to know more, Terry Teachout's biography Duke (2015) is superb in its research and, while Teachout has a few irritating quirks (such as a fetish for formal music training, which Ellington never received, and which Teachout sees as a major and serious failing), they are clearly his own personal opinions, and do little or no damage to the story of Ellington's life.

NPR also has a wonderful (if hagiographic) series of audio documentaries, Jazz Profiles, with several episodes dedicated to the Duke. Today I'll simply link to "Ellington the Composer - Pt. 1". This episode includes a downloadable MP3, so you can listen to it any time, which not all episodes do.
